domain: Disaster Anthropology / Institutional Memory / Land-Use Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the Aneyoshi tsunami stone's function as a land-use commitment system across 78 years (1933-2011). The stone inscription 'Do not build below this point' survived three generations without catastrophic testing, successfully protecting all 11 households in 2011 when surrounding communities were devastated. The kernel contest examines whether the stone retained live behavioral commitment or decayed to commemorative symbol.

key_entities: Aneyoshi village (11 households, fishing community, survived 2011 tsunami)
Tsunami stone (erected 1933, inscription warning against low-elevation building)
Village leadership (Tamishige Kimura, enforced ancestral rule)
Broader Sanriku coast communities (rebuilt at waterfront, ignored stones, devastated 2011)
Japanese government (built seawalls, alternative protection mechanism)
Intergenerational transmission system (school curriculum, oral tradition, spatial practice)
key_tensions: Economic convenience (proximity to fishing livelihood) vs safety compliance (steep hill climb daily)
Aneyoshi's sustained commitment vs broader coastal forgetting (stones became scenery)
Stone permanence vs three-generation memory decay (Imamura's catastrophe-theorem)
key_mechanisms: Spatial enforcement: stone placement on hillside creates daily visual reminder during transit
Educational transmission: stone studied in school curriculum (Yuto Kimura testimony)
Social enforcement: village leader describes rule 'no one dares break' (normative pressure)
key_absences: No documentation of enforcement mechanism when economic pressure to build lower emerged
No record of dissent or attempted violations during 78-year non-catastrophe period

axiom_contradictions.basis: Commemorative-husk reading requires accepting that symbolic reverence can coexist with behavioral non-compliance (stone honored but ignored). Behavioral-competence reading requires accepting that ancestral authority retains binding force across generations. No framework can hold both: either the stone constrains building or it does not.

omegas.description: No documentation of enforcement mechanism when economic pressure to build lower emerged. Was compliance voluntary or coerced? If voluntary, what sustained it across three generations?
No record of attempted violations during 78-year period. Kimura claims 'no one dares break' the rule, but absence of dissent documentation may reflect survivor bias or incomplete historical record.

Aneyoshi is exceptional. What conditions enabled sustained commitment when broader Sanriku coast forgot? Village size (11 households), fishing monoculture, leadership continuity, or stone placement specifics?
78 years without catastrophic testing is one data point. Would commitment have survived 150 years? 200? At what temporal distance does even spatial enforcement decay?
